Why can't liquid exist in vacuum?
vapour pressure point is a lot higher than vacuum, so it will evaporate. Even metals will evaporate.

Check out a phase diagram for materials - the phase diagram for water is a little unusual, so let's look at the general phase diagram concept instead. It's basically a chart of how the boiling/freezing temperatures change under the effects of pressure - which is exactly how to answer your question.

The temperature and pressure axes should make pretty good sense, but notice the location of the triple point is what matters here.

Liquid is a somewhat difficult phase for substances to be in - you need to balance the line between "so much energy, the particles fly around freely and become a gas" and the alternative, "so little energy, the particles stick together in a rigid solid structure."

A big part of what prevents the transition into gas phase is the pressure surrounding the substance - if liquid water is getting bombarded on all sides by high pressure gas atoms, it will require much more energy (higher temperature) to become a gas itself, due to all the competition.

As pressure goes down, it becomes easier and easier to become gas. Once you get down below the triple point, the boiling and melting points meet - and a liquid phase becomes impossible.
